newsitem.title: USA: Russians to OK START-2 nuclear cuts predicts Perry.
newsitem.headline: Russians to OK START-2 nuclear cuts predicts Perry.

text.p: Despite a hostile reception from Russian lawmakers in Moscow this week, U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry predicted on Friday that Russia's State Duma would ratify the START-2 nuclear arms reduction treaty within months.

"I am optimistic that when the decision time comes, the vote comes on this, which is probably several months from now, that the START-2 will be ratified in Russia," Perry told reporters flying home with him to Washington from a three-day visit to Russia.

He also said that Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov had assured him privately during talks that the West should have no concern about any rebellion by Russia's cash-strapped and struggling armed forces.

The U.S. Senate this year overwhelmingly ratified the START-2 treaty, which would slash long-range nuclear warheads in the United States and Russia to a third of Cold War levels. But Perry got a cold reception in a personal ratification plea to Duma members this week.

He told reporters on Friday that much of that outspoken opposition had come from Russian nationalists such as Vladimir Zhirinovsky, who did not want to give up nuclear arms. Perry said that such rockbound thinking was not in the mainstream of the lower house of parliament.

"That (ratification) is not going to be without a lot of debate, a lot of discussion, some clarifying points on the treaty which they are concerned about," Perry said. "But I would be willing to make a little side bet with any of you ... I think we're going to pull that through."

The treaty would reduce the current total of about 6,000 long-range warheads on each side to between 3,000 and 3,500 by the year 2003. Perry conceded that a major problem was Duma opposition to expansion of NATO into Eastern Europe but said the treaty would overcome that hurdle.

Although legislator after legislator spoke out against the treaty and peppered Perry with difficult questions, he said that his arguments on money-saving aspects of the treaty and his offer to quickly begin negotiating a START-3 treaty once ratification was completed might have swayed opinions.

"This represented to them a view of the START-2 that I don't believe they thought seriously about, and I have some confidence that in the months ahead that this will influence their thinking," he said.
Perry and Senator Joseph Lieberman, D-Connecticut, who made the trip with Perry, said negative statements from Zhirinovsky supporters did "by no means represent a consensus at the Duma."

Perry, who met twice with Rodionov this week and will meet with him again in November in Bosnia and in December in Washington, said that he was impressed by the minister and had been assured that Russian forces were not prepared to mutiny despite morale problems caused by delays in pay.
He said that speculation about a military uprising was, in Rodionov's words, "overblown."
"I would think that Minister Rodionov is in the best position to judge that and he said that is not a concern of his. He thinks that's quite overblown," the secretary said.

Earlier on Friday, Perry and Lieberman along with Senator Sam Nunn, D-Georgia, and Senator Richard Lugar, R-Indiana, visited Russia's frigid Severdovinsk Naval Base near the Arctic Circle where they watched a rusty nuclear missile submarine being cut up and compressed for scrap metal under the START-1 treaty.
"This was a very powerful personal experience," said Lieberman, calling it a perfect example of the beating swords into ploughshares.
